INFO.NAME: ICA0024 Concept glossary
INFO.INTRO: A study reference for Lectures 1-9. Terms explain the principles used in the questionnaires, without requiring product-specific syntax. Entries are grouped by the lecture that first explains them and ordered alphabetically within each group. A concept that returns in a later lecture is defined only once; a term in italics inside a definition refers to another entry.

ENTRY.DEFINITION: The observed condition of infrastructure at a particular time. It can differ from the desired state because of manual changes, failures, incomplete deployment, or changes outside the automation's control.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A metaphor for two ways of treating servers. Pets are unique, hand-maintained machines whose loss is a serious problem; cattle are interchangeable instances that are recreated from maintained definitions when they fail. Treating servers as cattle still requires their persistent data to be kept and recovered separately.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A difference between actual managed configuration and its intended baseline. A difference between environments is not automatically drift: explicitly approved differences, such as production capacity, can be intentional.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: The process of bringing actual state into agreement with desired state. Some tools converge only when someone runs them, while others keep comparing and correcting continuously, so drift between runs is handled differently. An operation that does nothing repeatedly may be idempotent but still fail to converge if the starting state is incorrect.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A description of the state that should exist, leaving automation to determine the necessary operations. Declaring a result does not eliminate dependencies or guarantee that every operation can run in parallel.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A relationship in which one resource or operation needs another resource or its output. For example, configuring a new server may require its assigned address. Expressing this relationship is more reliable than relying on file order or copied values.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: The intended condition of the resources being managed, expressed in maintained definitions and configuration values. It is the reference against which actual state is compared; it may describe only part of a system.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: The property that repeating an operation after it has reached its result produces no further state changes under unchanged relevant conditions. Checking state is compatible with idempotence. An unchanged result alone does not prove that the state is correct.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: An approach in which deployed instances are replaced with newly prepared instances when changes are needed. Persistent application data must survive replacement through separately managed storage or a tested migration or recovery process.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Instructions describing operations to perform and their order. Their effects can depend on the starting state. An imperative procedure can be designed to be idempotent; declarative and idempotent describe different properties.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A service model that provides infrastructure resources such as virtual machines, storage, and networking. Customers typically manage guest operating systems and application software; the precise responsibility boundary depends on the service.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Managing infrastructure through maintained, machine-readable definitions that can be versioned, reviewed, validated, and applied repeatedly. Keeping a file in version control does not by itself guarantee correct automation or reproducible external inputs.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Compute, storage, and network. Compute executes workloads, storage retains data, and networking connects resources. These are infrastructure capabilities rather than names of tools or deployment environments.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: An approach in which changes are applied to existing running instances. It can support targeted updates, but the process must manage drift and account for the state already present on each instance.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A service model that provides a managed platform for deploying applications. Compared with IaaS, more operating-system and runtime maintenance typically moves to the provider, while the application team retains responsibility for its application and requirements.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: The authoritative maintained definition or record for a particular kind of information. Dependent configuration should obtain that information through a clear relationship rather than through independently edited copies. Authority does not remove the need to inspect actual state.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Recording changes to definitions over time so they can be reviewed, compared, and traced. Restoring an earlier source revision can support recovery planning, but it does not automatically restore deleted data or reverse infrastructure changes safely.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 1: Infrastructure as Code concepts

ENTRY.DEFINITION: The image from which a machine or another image is created. Moving stable, rarely changing state into a shared base reduces later provisioning work, while derived images add workload-specific software. Updating the base does not automatically update derived images or running instances.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 2: Images and machine initialization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Configuration performed when an instance starts for the first time, often from instructions supplied to the platform when the instance is created, sometimes called user data. It typically provides identity or environment-specific values. A first-start action is not a continuous configuration check, and its output is often harder to inspect than a separate configuration run.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 2: Images and machine initialization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Software installation and configuration performed while preparing an image. The result becomes part of a reusable artifact. Common, relatively stable requirements are often prepared here to reduce repeated work when instances start.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 2: Images and machine initialization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: An isolated execution environment for application processes. Typical Linux containers share a host Linux kernel, unlike virtual machines with their own guest kernels. This affects compatibility and the isolation boundary; sharing a kernel does not mean having no isolation.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 2: Images and machine initialization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: An image prepared with selected organizational or workload-specific software and configuration. It can provide a tested common starting state and reduce launch-time setup. Its usefulness depends on maintaining and validating its build process.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 2: Images and machine initialization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A master image from which all machines of a given kind are started. If it is prepared by hand and captured as a snapshot, it collects undocumented changes and cannot be rebuilt reliably; if it is built automatically from maintained definitions, the same idea is sound. The name alone does not tell which of the two practices is used.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 2: Images and machine initialization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Software that provides and manages virtualized hardware on which virtual machines run. A hypervisor can run directly on physical hardware or within a host operating system, depending on its design.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 2: Images and machine initialization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Whether an image is suitable for a target platform, image format, and processor architecture. Equivalent intended software baselines may need different image artifacts for different targets; one image is not automatically portable everywhere.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 2: Images and machine initialization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: An organization of image definitions into shared bases and specialized descendants. It reduces duplicated baseline logic, but changes still require rebuilding and testing affected descendants and deliberately updating deployed instances.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 2: Images and machine initialization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A reusable artifact containing a starting operating-system and software state for a machine. Multiple instances can start from the same image and later diverge. Instance changes do not automatically modify the source image.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 2: Images and machine initialization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Application information that must outlive a process or replaceable instance, such as user records. Image replacement must account for this data separately; recreating software is not the same as recovering application data.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 2: Images and machine initialization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: The ability to recreate a system or artifact through a maintained, understood process rather than relying on undocumented manual changes. Rebuildability does not necessarily imply byte-for-byte identical output if the process uses changing external inputs.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 2: Images and machine initialization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: The ability to obtain the same specified result from controlled inputs and a defined process. For matching software versions, the base image and dependencies must be controlled as well as the instructions. Exact binary reproducibility may require additional controls.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 2: Images and machine initialization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A point-in-time capture of state, subject to the scope and consistency of the snapshot mechanism. It can support restoration or cloning, but does not explain how that state was constructed or replace maintained build definitions.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 2: Images and machine initialization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A supplied starting image, often provided by an operating-system or platform vendor. It can be used directly or customized. Its suitability and version still need to be selected and checked for the intended workload.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 2: Images and machine initialization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A machine-like environment with virtualized hardware and a guest operating system, including its own kernel. It consumes resources from an underlying host and can have a lifecycle independent of other virtual machines on that host.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 2: Images and machine initialization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Two ways for a configuration tool to reach managed machines. Agent-based tools run a helper process on every node, while agentless tools connect over existing remote-access protocols and push changes during a run. Agentless management is simpler to adopt, but the targets must still be reachable, accept the credentials, and provide what the tool needs to run there.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Determining whether relevant observed or generated configuration differs from the intended result. Meaningful checks can trigger necessary updates or reloads. The presence of a directory alone does not establish that the intended software version is installed.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Combining smaller configuration units into a complete deployment definition. The composition should make selected units, their inputs, and their relationships understandable; breaking a system into files does not automatically produce clear boundaries.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: An agreed starting set of settings and software requirements for a class of systems. A shared baseline can be combined with workload-specific requirements and approved environment differences. It must be maintained and checked against actual systems.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A value that intentionally replaces a default or a value from another configuration layer. Clear, documented precedence rules are needed to explain which value takes effect and to prevent hidden conflicts.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: An explicit input that varies the behavior of a reusable definition, such as capacity or an environment-specific endpoint. Parameters allow shared logic to remain common while keeping intended differences visible and reviewable.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A file with placeholders that are filled from variables and gathered facts before it is written to a target. It keeps one shared structure while letting values differ per host or group. Every placeholder needs a defined value in the run's context; a missing value should stop the run rather than produce an incomplete file.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Day 1 is the initial installation and configuration of a system; day 2 covers later maintenance such as updates, restarts, and cleanup. Initial setup can be mostly declarative, but maintenance often needs some imperative compensating actions, such as a restart after a configuration change. Treating day 2 as a repeat of day 1 can miss these follow-up steps.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A value used when no higher-priority value is supplied under the configuration scheme's rules. Useful defaults simplify reuse, but they should not conceal required choices or make the effective configuration hard to understand.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Values and deliberate variations associated with an environment such as development or production. Keeping these separate from shared logic makes differences easier to review without independently maintaining complete copies of the same definitions.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Checking that the system performs an intended behavior, such as serving a user request or accessing its database. Successful configuration operations do not by themselves establish that the full application works.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A named selection of machines sharing a relevant purpose or property, such as web servers or all machines in one environment. Groups help apply common configuration broadly and specialized configuration only to the appropriate targets.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A maintained representation of managed hosts, groups, and relevant targeting information. It supports selecting and reaching configuration targets. It may be supplied statically or derived from current infrastructure information and is not a complete snapshot of server state.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Managing only the resources or properties explicitly included in the automation's scope. Unmentioned resources may remain unmanaged; their omission is not automatically a request to remove them or proof that they meet a complete baseline.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A coherent package of configuration responsibilities and supporting resources, sometimes called a role or module. Clear inputs and boundaries support reuse and focused maintenance. Units can still depend on one another and need integration checks.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Organizing definitions around distinct responsibilities, for example keeping the list of managed machines, the configuration data for groups and hosts, and the configuration code apart so that each can change independently. This can improve ownership and review without requiring separate products or repositories for every concern.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A reload asks a service to reread configuration where that behavior is supported; a restart stops and starts the service. The appropriate action depends on the service and change. Running either action unconditionally can introduce unnecessary work or disruption.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 3: Server state and configuration organization

ENTRY.DEFINITION: An automated check placed around configuration code, such as a test, linter, or policy, that must pass before a change moves on; also called a guardrail. Because configuration is code, it can be checked by code, including code produced by an AI assistant. A safeguard reduces risk only as far as its checks reflect the behavior that actually matters.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 4: Resilience and verifying configuration code

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A physically separate data-centre location within a cloud region, which is a geographic area made up of several such zones. Spreading instances across zones lets a service survive the loss of one zone. Placing everything in one zone, or depending on a single shared component, still leaves a single point of failure.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 4: Resilience and verifying configuration code

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Deliberately and repeatedly introducing failures, such as stopping random servers, disabling a whole zone, or simulating traffic spikes, to show that a system recovers without users noticing. It turns resilience from an assumption into something that is tested regularly. It is only safe when recovery is automated and the impact of each experiment is understood.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 4: Resilience and verifying configuration code

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Running configuration code both against a freshly prepared machine and against one that has already been configured. Repeated runs on one long-lived machine can hide steps that only work because of earlier manual or partial changes. A cleanup procedure can make this faster, but a full rebuild remains the final check.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 4: Resilience and verifying configuration code

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A situation in which two definitions manage the same resource with different intended values, such as one directory with two different owners. Each run then changes the resource back and forth, so the code never reaches a stable result and appears not to be idempotent. Every managed property should have one clear owner.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 4: Resilience and verifying configuration code

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Keeping the time between making a change and seeing its tested result short, for example with quick resets and targeted runs. Problems are then found while the change is still fresh. Speed does not replace the slower, complete checks needed before a release.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 4: Resilience and verifying configuration code

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A static analysis tool that checks code against rules for style, structure, maintainability, and risky constructs, beyond basic syntax. Its findings often point to code smells: signs that code is fragile or hard to maintain even though it runs. A clean linter result does not show that the configuration produces a working system.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 4: Resilience and verifying configuration code

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Deliberately stopping, restarting, or deleting a server or environment to check that it comes back in a working state. Once recovery is proven, monitoring can restart or replace failed machines automatically. A configuration that works only until the next reboot has not passed a recovery test.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 4: Resilience and verifying configuration code

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Stopping a resource that seems unused and waiting to see whether anyone or anything reports a problem. It also checks whether monitoring and alerting react to an outage. Silence is weak evidence, so the resource should remain recoverable in case a rarely used dependency appears later.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 4: Resilience and verifying configuration code

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Keeping private keys, passwords, and tokens out of committed code, for example by excluding them with an ignore file and supplying them from a protected store when needed. Deleting a committed secret in a later change does not remove it from the repository history, so an exposed secret must be replaced. Committed secrets are usually the first issue a security review flags.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 4: Resilience and verifying configuration code

ENTRY.DEFINITION: An operation that inspects the actual state of a resource and changes only what differs, such as a package or service management step. A generic command guarded only by a check for an existing file is weaker, because the file can exist while the resource is still wrong. Generic commands remain a fallback when no state-aware operation exists.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 4: Resilience and verifying configuration code

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Applying changes during normal operation without users noticing, for example by preparing a new version alongside the old one and switching traffic once it is healthy (blue-green deployment). It reduces reliance on announced maintenance windows. It requires redundancy, health checks, and changes that old and new versions can tolerate at the same time.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 4: Resilience and verifying configuration code

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Infrastructure whose resources are exposed as objects that programs create, read, update, and delete through an API. These calls are imperative: a script must know which calls to make and in which order. Declarative tools use the same API but work out the calls from the described result.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 5: Declarative cloud provisioning and state

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A lookup that reads information about existing resources managed elsewhere, such as a network, its subnets, or the latest suitable image, without creating anything. It avoids copying identifiers into code by hand. Its result can change between runs, for example when a newer image is published.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 5: Declarative cloud provisioning and state

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A preview of what a run would add, change, or destroy, produced by comparing the code, the recorded state, and the real infrastructure. Some changes cannot be made in place, so the plan shows the resource being destroyed and recreated. A plan should be read before it is applied, and it describes intended operations rather than guaranteeing that they will succeed.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 5: Declarative cloud provisioning and state

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A periodic probe that a load balancer or platform uses to decide whether a node can receive traffic. A node that fails several consecutive checks is taken out of rotation until it recovers. A health check proves only what it tests, so a shallow check can pass while the application is still broken.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 5: Declarative cloud provisioning and state

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A single, stable entry point that spreads traffic across several nodes, absorbs spikes, and lets nodes be replaced without clients noticing. In a cloud it is usually assembled from several related resources, such as listeners, target groups, and network rules. It is a resource with its own cost and failure modes, not just a setting.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 5: Declarative cloud provisioning and state

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A provider-operated service, such as a managed database, that takes care of tasks like clustering, backups, and upgrades. It trades money and some control for less operational work than installing the same software on virtual machines. The consumer still configures it, secures access to it, and remains responsible for its data.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 5: Declarative cloud provisioning and state

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A plug-in that connects a declarative provisioning tool to one API, such as a cloud, DNS, or monitoring service, and exposes that API's objects as resources. Several providers can be combined in one project. A provider reflects the platform's own resource model, so much of the complexity comes from the platform rather than from the tool.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 5: Declarative cloud provisioning and state

ENTRY.DEFINITION: An imperative step, such as running commands or copying files, attached to a declaratively managed resource. It typically runs only when the resource is created, so later changes to the step are not applied to existing resources. Preparing an image or using a configuration tool is usually more predictable than mixing the two approaches.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 5: Declarative cloud provisioning and state

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Recorded state kept in shared storage outside an individual workstation, so that a team works from the same record. Only one run should change it at a time, which is usually enforced with locking. It must be protected like the infrastructure itself, because state can contain sensitive values.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 5: Declarative cloud provisioning and state

ENTRY.DEFINITION: The basic unit of declarative provisioning code: a resource type from a provider, a local name used for references, and attributes describing the desired object. It plays a role similar to a single task in server configuration. The local name identifies the definition in code and is not necessarily the resource's name on the platform.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 5: Declarative cloud provisioning and state

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A tool's record of the objects it created and their identifiers, used together with the code and the real infrastructure to decide what to change. Because of it, a resource removed from the code is destroyed, whereas tools without recorded state need an explicit cleanup step. Recorded state can still differ from reality and can contain secrets, so it does not replace inspecting actual state.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 5: Declarative cloud provisioning and state

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Dividing infrastructure into several projects, each with its own state, for example by layer or by how often its parts change. Smaller states let teams work without blocking each other and limit the effect of a mistake. Values needed across the split must then be shared through explicit outputs or lookups rather than direct references.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 5: Declarative cloud provisioning and state

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A resource that is created only when an input enables it, for example an optional load balancer that is switched off by default. Inputs can then control the shape and cost of an environment without separate copies of the code. Each combination of options is a different configuration that needs to be tested.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 6: Choosing cloud deployment options

ENTRY.DEFINITION: The packaged application with its dependencies, from which containers are started. The same image can be run by functions, container services, virtual machines, or clusters, which keeps deployment options open. The term is wider than any one container engine, and the image still needs permissions, configuration, and a runtime environment around it.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 6: Choosing cloud deployment options

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A service that stores and distributes container images; it can be public, self-hosted, or provided by the cloud. Private application images belong in a private registry, which can be defined as code together with rules such as how many images to retain. A registry used by several deployments is shared infrastructure and may deserve its own project and state (see State splitting).

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 6: Choosing cloud deployment options

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A compute option in which the provider runs container images as tasks or services without exposing the underlying machines. A task definition describes how to run a container, while a service keeps the intended number of copies running. An always-running container is paid for even when it receives no requests.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 6: Choosing cloud deployment options

ENTRY.DEFINITION: An application design made of small handlers that react to events such as requests, messages, or schedules. It fits functions well because each reaction can run independently. A monolithic application usually fits better in one long-running container, virtual machine, or cluster.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 6: Choosing cloud deployment options

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A compute option in which the platform runs code, packaged as an archive or container image for a supported runtime, in response to events such as HTTP requests or schedules. The platform starts more function instances as concurrent requests grow and removes them when traffic stops. Execution-time and runtime limits make it unsuitable for some long-running work.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 6: Choosing cloud deployment options

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A container orchestration cluster, such as managed Kubernetes, whose control plane is operated by the provider. It can handle far larger and more complex workloads than a few containers need. It still includes virtual machines and usually a load balancer, so it costs more and brings more operational responsibility.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 6: Choosing cloud deployment options

ENTRY.DEFINITION: An event emitted on a schedule by a separate platform service to start a function or container task. Moving scheduling out of the application means compute runs, and is paid for, only when the job runs. The scheduler needs its own permission to start its target.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 6: Choosing cloud deployment options

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A platform service that stores secrets, such as passwords or keys, which applications read by name at run time instead of having them in code or images. The application needs explicit permission to read each secret. Values passed through provisioning code can still end up in recorded state unless the tool supports values that are not stored.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 6: Choosing cloud deployment options

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Compute options in which the platform hides the machines, so users deal with code, permissions, and integrations rather than servers. Functions and containers as a service are both examples. Servers still exist, and their limits, costs, and failure modes still affect the design.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 6: Choosing cloud deployment options

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Paying for resources while they run or handle work, such as function execution time, rather than for capacity that is always on. Idle usage-based resources can cost little or nothing, while always-on resources such as load balancers or running machines cost money even without traffic. A small change in code can therefore produce a large change in cost.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 6: Choosing cloud deployment options

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Access rights granted to applications and services rather than to people, ideally narrowed to exactly what they need, such as one secret or one image repository. When resources are created through code, nothing is granted by default, not even writing logs, whereas an interactive console may add such permissions silently. Missing permissions are a common reason why code that imitates a console setup fails.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 6: Choosing cloud deployment options

ENTRY.DEFINITION: An automated sequence that runs on every change: fast checks such as linters, policy checks, and smoke tests first, then delivery to a first environment such as staging with integration and monitoring checks, and only then production. Ordering stages from cheap to expensive gives early feedback. A pipeline enforces only the checks it actually contains.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 7: Modules, versioning and automated quality checks

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Copying the code of an existing, often inactive, third-party module into your own codebase, adapting it, and maintaining it yourself. It preserves useful work when the original project no longer meets your needs. From then on, fixes and security updates are your own responsibility.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 7: Modules, versioning and automated quality checks

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A test that applies infrastructure code to real or realistic targets, such as containers or virtual machines with different operating systems, and checks the result. It catches what usually breaks in practice, such as package names that differ between distributions. It needs test images, machines or runners, and a way to create and destroy throwaway targets.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 7: Modules, versioning and automated quality checks

ENTRY.DEFINITION: The set of inputs and defaults through which consumers configure a reusable configuration unit. It is the contract that versioning protects, so changing it can break consumers. A module with hundreds of inputs often indicates the wrong abstraction; several focused modules are usually easier to use.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 7: Modules, versioning and automated quality checks

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Judging a third-party module before adopting it: how active it is, how quickly issues and security problems are fixed, how its interface has evolved, who maintains it, and whether it has documentation, examples, and tests. Popularity and download counts show the scale of use, not suitability. An adopted module becomes part of your own infrastructure's risk.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 7: Modules, versioning and automated quality checks

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A shared library where reusable modules or roles are published, discovered, and downloaded. It makes existing work easy to find and reuse. Publication in a registry does not guarantee quality, so each module still needs a module quality assessment.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 7: Modules, versioning and automated quality checks

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Organization-wide rules, such as required tags, approved providers, or size and security limits, written as code and checked automatically by a policy engine. A violation can produce a warning or stop the pipeline before the change reaches infrastructure. Policies check rules about the code, not whether the deployed system works.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 7: Modules, versioning and automated quality checks

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Restructuring code to improve its boundaries and clarity, for example by extracting repeated logic into modules, without changing its intended result. Code that keeps growing without restructuring becomes hard for people and AI assistants to change safely. Refactoring relies on tests that show the behavior is preserved.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 7: Modules, versioning and automated quality checks

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A versioning scheme of major.minor.patch numbers. A patch release must not change the interface, a minor release may add backward-compatible functionality, and only a major release may introduce breaking changes. The scheme is a promise kept by people and checks; the numbers alone do not prove compatibility.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 7: Modules, versioning and automated quality checks

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Running the same tests against several target environments or parameter sets, such as different operating-system distributions, with one run per combination. It shows where behavior differs between targets. Each added dimension multiplies the cost, so the matrix should cover the targets that matter to the module's users.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 7: Modules, versioning and automated quality checks

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A fast, local test of logic in isolation from real resources. For infrastructure code it often adds little, because much of the logic is already validated by the tool and real failures appear on real targets. It is not a substitute for an integration test.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 7: Modules, versioning and automated quality checks

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Referring to an exact module version rather than the latest release or a version range. Pinning lets maintainers release freely while each consumer decides when to upgrade. Pinned versions still need deliberate, tested upgrades, or consumers fall behind on fixes.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 7: Modules, versioning and automated quality checks

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A place where released versions, such as modules, images, or application packages, are stored and distributed, for example as version-control tags, release pages, or files on a server. It isolates consumers from ongoing development because they use only published versions. The repository is itself infrastructure that must be maintained and protected.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 8: Module versioning and interface design

ENTRY.DEFINITION: An isolated context that delivers an application's resources and dependencies, such as development, staging, or production. There is no universal definition: its scope depends on the organization, team, and scale. Creating every environment from the same module with different parameters reduces drift and keeps lower environments useful for testing (see Environment-specific configuration).

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 8: Module versioning and interface design

ENTRY.DEFINITION: An input designed to let consumers add behavior without changing a module, such as a list of virtual hosts passed to a web-server role. It applies the open-closed principle. Each extension point becomes part of the interface and must be maintained.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 8: Module versioning and interface design

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A module, role, or package published by a community or vendor and imported rather than written in-house. A well-maintained one saves code, effort, and testing, and a large interface can be justified by wide use and sensible defaults. It still needs a module quality assessment and version pinning.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 8: Module versioning and interface design

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A published version that is never changed after release; further work goes into new versions. Consumers can then rely on a version meaning the same code every time. Moving or reusing a version label breaks that guarantee.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 8: Module versioning and interface design

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A module written within an organization to encode its own conventions, such as sizing, tagging, security, and network layout. It is most useful for concepts specific to the organization, after checking what existing providers and modules already offer. Its authors know its consumers, so it usually needs fewer inputs than a public module, but it still needs tests and a release process.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 8: Module versioning and interface design

ENTRY.DEFINITION: The promises a module makes through its interface: every input is a commitment that its author must keep working in later versions. Supporting very different cases, such as two database engines in one module, creates a different contract that usually belongs in a separate module. A smaller contract is easier to test and to keep stable.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 8: Module versioning and interface design

ENTRY.DEFINITION: The producer is the team that develops, tests, and releases a module; consumers are the teams or projects that use it. Consumers choose which version to use and when to upgrade, and their needs should shape the interface. A producer that also uses its own module notices problems earlier, but that does not replace considering how others use it.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 8: Module versioning and interface design

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A design rule stating that a module should be open for extension, through its inputs, but closed for modification, so consumers rarely need to change its code. It is applied with the knowledge available when the module is designed. Later needs may still require refactoring and a new version.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 8: Module versioning and interface design

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Adding inputs for things that never differ between consumers, or wrapping a single resource in a module that exposes almost all of its settings. It adds complexity and testing effort without adding value. A useful first rule is to parameterize what affects security, size, and naming and to fix the rest.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 8: Module versioning and interface design

ENTRY.DEFINITION: The automated steps a module goes through before publication: integration tests on test infrastructure, static and policy analysis, a publish step, and often a notification to consumers. In version control, tagging a commit can define the version number that consumers reference. Without such a process, a version number says nothing about which checks the code passed.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 8: Module versioning and interface design

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Keeping software patching separate from module design by exposing package or image versions as inputs. A security fix then becomes a change of value rather than a change of module code. A new module release is still needed when the fix changes the module's structure.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 8: Module versioning and interface design

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A practice of delivering changes frequently and reliably through automation, small batches, and built-in quality checks. It began in software development but depends on suitable infrastructure and on development and operations working together. Automating one step does not achieve it if changes still wait in queues between teams.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 9: GitOps, pipelines and team workflows

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A component inside or near the infrastructure that repeatedly checks that the real state still matches the definitions in version control and corrects differences (see Convergence). It is sometimes treated as the fourth GitOps principle and is common on container platforms. It is optional: scheduled pipeline runs can provide much of the same checking.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 9: GitOps, pipelines and team workflows

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Applying the same version-control and pipeline workflow to anything that can be described as text, such as documentation, dashboards, alerts, service-level objectives, and security policies. It brings review, history, and automated checks to those artifacts. Each kind of artifact still needs suitable validation.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 9: GitOps, pipelines and team workflows

ENTRY.DEFINITION: How a change moves from the team that needs it to production. Separate team silos, tickets, and repeated questions can make a five-minute change take days. Improving the flow means removing waiting and handovers, not only automating the technical step.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 9: GitOps, pipelines and team workflows

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Managing infrastructure and configuration through declarative configuration kept under version control in Git, with automated pipelines that verify and deliver every change. It is continuous delivery applied to infrastructure code and is not limited to container platforms. Keeping code in Git is not GitOps if changes are still applied by hand.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 9: GitOps, pipelines and team workflows

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A pipeline definition stored as code in the same repository as the infrastructure it delivers, and owned by that repository's team. It is reviewed and versioned like the rest of the code. Its checks act as guardrails that codify the owning team's rules (see Automated safeguard).

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 9: GitOps, pipelines and team workflows

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A proposed change on a separate branch, submitted for review to a repository, including one owned by another team. Pipelines check it without deploying it, people discuss it, and the owners merge it, which triggers delivery. It replaces ticket-based requests but still depends on timely review.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 9: GitOps, pipelines and team workflows

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A delivery model in which an agent inside or near the infrastructure periodically fetches definitions from version control and applies them. The pipeline service then needs no direct access to the target. The agent holds broad permissions close to the infrastructure and must itself be secured and monitored.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 9: GitOps, pipelines and team workflows

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A delivery model in which a pipeline service runs provisioning or configuration tools and pushes changes into the target. Each change is a visible pipeline run, which makes it easy to follow. The pipeline environment needs network access and credentials for the infrastructure, which is a security concern, especially for externally hosted services.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 9: GitOps, pipelines and team workflows

ENTRY.DEFINITION: Keeping the publication of a tested application version apart from the decision about where it runs. Application pipelines publish artifacts to an artifact repository, while the infrastructure repository records which version runs in each environment. Version updates can be committed automatically, so that repository has both human and automated authors.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 9: GitOps, pipelines and team workflows

ENTRY.DEFINITION: The arrangement in which the team that owns a repository defines its structure, pipelines, and rules, such as linter settings, and only that team merges to the main branch. Other teams contribute through pull requests. Consistency within the team matters more than any particular style rule.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 9: GitOps, pipelines and team workflows

ENTRY.DEFINITION: A simple, documented way for other teams to make frequent changes themselves, such as editing structured data files in a repository or using a self-service portal. The internals can remain as complex as the owning team needs. Without automated checks behind it, self-service only moves risk to another team.

CATEGORY.NAME: Lecture 9: GitOps, pipelines and team workflows
